replies.author: @karolnewman85
replies.text:
​@konstantin1028Listing real dates doesn't make the conclusion true. You are leaving out the exact details that make 1939 completely different from everything else you mentioned:

1. The Secret Protocol: None of the earlier treaties (1934 Polish-German, Munich, or Baltic pacts) included a secret deal to invade and carve up neighboring countries. The Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact had a Secret Additional Protocol where Hitler and Stalin explicitly divided Poland, Finland, Romania, and the Baltic states between themselves. (Also, the USSR signed a non-aggression pact with Poland in 1932 and broke it).

2. Poland & Czechoslovakia (1938): In 1919, while Poland was fighting Soviet Russia, Czechoslovakia seized Zaolzie—a small, Polish-majority border strip. In October 1938, after Britain and France handed the Sudetenland to Hitler at Munich, Poland took Zaolzie back so Germany wouldn't grab it. It was an opportunistic diplomatic mistake, not a coordinated Nazi-Polish alliance to destroy a country. As for "blocking Soviet aid": the USSR didn't even border Czechoslovakia. Neither Poland nor Romania trusted the Red Army to leave once let onto their soil (which 1939–1940 proved right), and the 1935 Soviet-Czechoslovak treaty only required Stalin to intervene if France fought first—which France refused to do.

3. Poland had not "ceased to exist" on Sept 17: That was Molotov's propaganda excuse. On September 17, the Polish army was still actively fighting—Warsaw didn't fall until Sept 28, and the last major battle (Kock) lasted until October 6. The Polish government was still inside Poland on Sept 17 and only crossed into Romania late that night because the Red Army invaded from the east.

4. Joint Invasion: Sending over 600,000 troops across a border, fighting Polish forces, taking 250,000 POWs, and holding a joint victory parade with the Wehrmacht in Brest-Litovsk on September 22 isn't "entering an empty space"—it's a coordinated invasion.
